title: DOES LUST ALWAYS WANT SOMETHING? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT YOUR HEART IS REALLY HUNGRY FOR
paragraphs: DOES LUST ALWAYS WANT SOMETHING? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT YOUR HEART IS REALLY HUNGRY FOR

Sometimes lust isn't just craving another body. Sometimes it's a wounded heart searching for comfort, a lonely soul begging to feel wanted, and a spiritual battle you keep losing because you've been fighting the symptom while ignoring the wound. But what if Jesus wants to heal something deeper than the desire you've been ashamed to confess?
There is a kind of hunger that doesn't disappear after you feed it.
You know what I'm talking about.
You promised yourself you wouldn't go back.
Not tonight.
Not after everything God has brought you through.
Not after that prayer you prayed with tears running down your face.
But then the room became quiet.
Your phone was within reach.
Your thoughts started wandering.
And somewhere between loneliness, curiosity, exhaustion, and temptation, you found yourself standing at the same door you swore you would never open again.
Maybe you opened it.
Maybe you didn't.
Maybe nobody knows how close you came.
But you know.
And God knows.
And here's the question that might change how you understand your struggle:
What if the thing you're lusting after isn't the only thing you're hungry for?
What if you're reaching for pleasure because you don't know what to do with pain?
What if you're craving attention because somewhere inside, you're terrified of being forgotten?
What if you keep wanting someone to desire you because you've never really believed you were valuable without being desired?
And what if the enemy has learned to exploit legitimate human longings by offering you something that can never truly satisfy them?
Stay with me.
Because this isn't another article telling you to simply stop looking, stop thinking, stop feeling, and somehow become holy through sheer determination.
This is about the difference between a desire that belongs to our humanity and a desire that has begun ruling our hearts.
It's about the moment a longing becomes a master.
It's about the scandal of what we sometimes do in secret.
And the astonishing grace of a Savior who already knows the truth and still calls sinners to come into the light.
But before we go any further, we need to answer the question.
Does lust always want something?
Yes. But what lust consciously wants and what may be driving it beneath the surface are not always the same thing.
And misunderstanding that difference can leave someone fighting the same battle for years.
In the Greek New Testament, one important word translated as lust or desire is ἐπιθυμία (epithymia).
It refers to desire, longing, or craving.
Here is something many people overlook.
The word itself does not always describe sinful desire.
In Luke 22:15, Jesus uses the related verb ἐπεθύμησα (epethymēsa) when He tells His disciples that He has earnestly desired to eat the Passover with them before His suffering.
Jesus desired.
And Jesus never sinned.
That matters.
Because desire itself is not automatically evil.
The desire for intimacy is not evil.
The longing to be loved is not evil.
Sexual attraction is not automatically lust.
Wanting companionship does not make you impure.
And feeling lonely does not mean you have failed God.

The problem begins when desire turns away from God's good purposes and seeks satisfaction through what He forbids, when another person becomes an object to consume, or when a craving begins demanding obedience that belongs to God alone.
James 1:14–15 says:
"But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death." (KJV)
James is not describing every human longing as sinful.
He is describing the deadly progression of desire when it entices a person toward evil.
Notice the movement.
Desire.
Enticement.
Sin.
Death.
Something begins inside before it becomes visible outside.
And sometimes the most dangerous moment isn't when you commit the sin.
It's when you begin negotiating with it.
When you tell yourself one glance won't matter.
One conversation is harmless.
One private message isn't betrayal.
One fantasy isn't hurting anybody.
One more time, and then you'll repent.
But sin has a way of making tomorrow sound like a wonderful day to obey God while convincing you that tonight belongs to your appetite.
And suddenly, what began as a passing temptation becomes a carefully protected secret.
A secret that starts shaping your habits.
Your relationships.
Your prayer life.
Your conscience.
Even the way you see other people.
Jesus addresses this with unsettling clarity in Matthew 5:28:
"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." (KJV)
The Greek phrase πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn) expresses looking with the purpose of lusting after her.
Jesus is confronting more than involuntary awareness of someone's beauty.
He is exposing the deliberate cultivation of a covetous, sexually possessive gaze.
He is telling us that righteousness cannot be reduced to what our hands have or haven't done.
God cares about what our hearts are choosing.
And that truth is uncomfortable.
Because many people have never physically crossed a boundary while repeatedly crossing it in their imagination.
Some have remained outwardly faithful while inwardly feeding fantasies of someone who isn't their spouse.
Some have never touched pornography but have learned to consume people through social media, imagination, or flirtation.
And some have spent years convincing themselves that because nobody else knows, nothing serious is happening.
But secrecy doesn't turn sin into innocence.
It only hides the evidence from other people.
Not from God.
Yet here is where we must be careful.
Not every unwanted sexual thought is a chosen sin.
Not every intrusive image represents the true desire of your heart.
Not every experience of attraction is rebellion against God.
Temptation and surrender are not the same thing.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
If temptation itself were identical to sin, that verse would make no sense.
So don't confuse the arrival of temptation with the decision to welcome it.
The battle is not necessarily lost because a thought appeared.
What matters is what you choose to do with it.
Do you entertain it?
Feed it?
Return to it?
Arrange opportunities for it?
Or do you bring it before Christ and turn away?
And now we come to something even more personal.
Sometimes lust is not merely pursuing pleasure. Sometimes it is trying to escape something painful.
For one person, the struggle intensifies after rejection.
For another, it appears after a stressful day.
For another, it grows during seasons of loneliness.
For someone else, it becomes a way to feel powerful after spending the day feeling insignificant.
Sometimes the underlying experience is boredom.
Sometimes insecurity.
Sometimes anger.
Sometimes grief.
Sometimes a desire for reassurance.
And sometimes lust is exactly what it appears to be: a sinful appetite seeking forbidden gratification, without any deeper psychological explanation required.
We must not romanticize sin by assuming every sinful choice is secretly an untreated wound.
The Bible holds us responsible for our choices.
But Scripture also recognizes the complexity of the human heart.
Proverbs 20:5 says:
"Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out." (KJV)
Human motives are not always obvious, even to the person experiencing them.
And this is why someone can genuinely hate a pattern of sin while continuing to return to it.
They may understand that the behavior is wrong without understanding all the situations, beliefs, habits, and emotional triggers that make it so attractive.
Picture someone sitting alone at 1:17 in the morning.
They've spent the whole day being strong.
Strong for their family.
Strong at work.
Strong at church.
Strong for everyone who needed them.
But nobody asked how they were doing.
Nobody noticed their exhaustion.
Nobody saw the disappointment they swallowed.
And now the silence feels unbearable.
So they reach for their phone.
Not necessarily because they woke up that morning determined to rebel against God.
Perhaps they want relief.
A distraction.
A moment of excitement.
A temporary escape from feeling invisible.
But instead of bringing their exhaustion into the presence of God, they turn toward something that promises immediate comfort without requiring vulnerability.
For a moment, it works.
The mind becomes occupied.
The body responds.
The loneliness seems quieter.
Then the moment passes.
And the original pain is still there.
Only now, guilt may have joined it.
And the cycle begins again.
If that sounds familiar, I want you to understand something.
Recognizing the emotional circumstances surrounding sin does not excuse the sin.
It helps reveal where repentance, healing, wisdom, and practical change may all be necessary.
You cannot heal a wound by pretending it isn't there.
And you cannot overcome sin by pretending it isn't sin.
Both truths matter.
This is where the story of the Samaritan woman becomes so powerful.
In John 4, Jesus meets a woman at Jacob's well.
She comes to draw water.
A completely ordinary activity.
But this encounter becomes one of the most extraordinary conversations in the Gospel of John.
Jesus asks her for a drink.
Then He begins speaking about living water.
In John 4:13–14, He says:

"Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life." (KJV)
In the Greek text, the phrase ὕδωρ ζῶν (hydōr zōn) means "living water."
In ordinary usage, it could describe flowing or fresh water.
But Jesus uses the image to reveal something far greater: the life He gives, ultimately understood in John's Gospel in connection with the Holy Spirit.
He is not offering a temporary emotional high.
He is speaking of eternal life that comes through Him.
Then the conversation becomes painfully personal.
Jesus tells her to call her husband.
She says she has no husband.
Jesus reveals that she has had five husbands and that the man she currently has is not her husband.
Now, we must not add details Scripture never gives us.
The text does not tell us that she was sexually addicted.
It does not tell us why her marriages ended.
It does not tell us that every relationship was the result of lust.
It does not even tell us that she came to the well at that hour because the community had rejected her.
Those are common assumptions, not established facts.
What Scripture does show is that Jesus knew the complicated truth of her relational life.
And He did not walk away.
He exposed what was true without reducing her identity to her history.
He spoke about worship.
He revealed Himself as the Messiah.
And the woman went back to her community declaring:
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" (John 4:29, KJV)
Think about that.
The very things Jesus knew about her did not prevent her from inviting others to meet Him.
Her encounter with truth became the beginning of her testimony.
And many Samaritans believed through her witness.
This is what grace can do.
Grace does not need to falsify your history to give you a future.
It doesn't need to call darkness light.
It doesn't need to pretend your choices never mattered.
Grace brings you to the One who knows everything and can still make you new.
And perhaps that is what frightens us most.
Not merely that God knows our sin.
But that coming to Him means surrendering our right to keep protecting it.
Because sometimes we say we want freedom when what we really want is relief from consequences.
We want peace without confession.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Intimacy with God without surrendering our favorite escape.
We want Jesus to remove the shame while allowing the secret to remain untouched.
But Jesus loves us too much to become the guardian of our hidden chains.
He came to save us from sin, not to help us become comfortable living under its power.
Listen to what He says in John 8:34–36:
"Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin... If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed." (KJV)
The freedom Jesus gives is not merely the ability to feel less guilty.
It is freedom from sin's dominion.
Freedom to obey.
Freedom to love without consuming.
Freedom to see people as image-bearers rather than objects.
Freedom to tell the truth when hiding would be easier.
Freedom to stop worshiping a craving that has never been able to save you.
And that brings us to a painful question.
Have you ever noticed how lust can promise intimacy while training your heart to avoid it?
Real intimacy requires honesty.
Patience.
Respect.
Commitment.
Self-giving love.
It requires recognizing another person as a whole human being, with a soul, a history, boundaries, fears, and dignity.
Lust, by contrast, can reduce someone to the role they play in satisfying your appetite.
It asks, "What can I get?"
Love asks, "How can I honor?"
Lust can become impatient when gratification is delayed.
Love knows how to wait.
Lust can flourish in secrecy and fantasy.
Love seeks truth and faithfulness.
This does not mean genuine love has no physical desire.
God created human sexuality, and Scripture honors its rightful expression within marriage.
The Song of Songs openly celebrates marital desire.
But biblical love refuses to separate desire from holiness, dignity, and faithfulness.
First Corinthians 13:5 says that love "seeketh not her own."
That doesn't mean love never experiences personal longing.
It means love is not governed by selfish insistence.
And if your desire requires you to betray someone, deceive someone, objectify someone, manipulate someone, or violate God's commands, it is not made righteous simply because the feelings are intense.
Intensity is not proof of love.
Chemistry is not proof of God's approval.
And an open door is not always a door God wants you to walk through.
Sometimes the strongest act of love is refusing to take what you have no right to possess.
Sometimes the most courageous thing a person can do is close the conversation.
Delete the secret account.
End the inappropriate relationship.
Confess the hidden pattern.
Ask for accountability.
Seek pastoral help or qualified counseling when the struggle has become deeply entrenched.
Not because any of those actions earn salvation.
But because repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward God in a way that changes what you choose today.
The Hebrew word שׁוּב (shuv) carries the sense of turning or returning.
It appears in many Old Testament passages calling people to return to the Lord.
And the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated "repentance," speaks of a change of mind or heart that, in biblical context, calls for a changed direction.
Repentance is more than an emotional breakdown.
It is more than crying after getting caught.
It is more than promising never to do it again.
It is a turning from sin toward the living God.
And that turning may require difficult, practical decisions.
Because you cannot keep arranging your life around temptation and then act surprised when temptation keeps finding you.
You may need to stop following accounts that deliberately feed your fantasies.
You may need to establish boundaries with someone whose attention has become an emotional addiction.
You may need to stop bringing your phone into the same private situations where you repeatedly compromise.
You may need to admit to a mature, trustworthy believer that your struggle has become more serious than you've allowed anyone to know.
And if pornography or compulsive sexual behavior has become difficult to control, professional support can be part of wise, responsible care alongside spiritual discipleship.
None of this means that every believer will experience immediate victory.
Growth can be difficult.
Old habits may take time to dismantle.
But difficulty does not make obedience meaningless.
And repeated failure should never become an excuse to stop pursuing Christ.
First Corinthians 10:13 reminds believers that God is faithful and provides a way to endure temptation.
That promise is not a guarantee that temptation will feel easy.
It is a call to depend upon God's faithfulness rather than surrendering to the claim that sin is inevitable.
Now let me speak to the person who has already fallen.
The person reading this with a tightness in their chest.
The person who has confessed the same sin so many times that the words "Lord, forgive me" have started to feel painfully familiar.
You might be thinking:
How many times can I ask for forgiveness before God gets tired of hearing my voice?
How can I call myself a Christian when I still struggle with this?
What if I'm only pretending?
What if I've gone too far?
Please hear what Scripture actually says.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
And Romans 8:1 says:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." (KJV)
These promises are not permission to continue deliberately in sin.
Romans 6:1–2 explicitly rejects that idea.
They are assurances that the grace of God is greater than the accusation that repentant sinners are beyond His mercy.
The foundation of forgiveness is not the emotional intensity of your apology.
It is the finished work of Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely offer humanity motivational advice.
He bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
And He rose again.
The sinless Savior accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
First Peter 2:24 says He "bare our sins in his own body on the tree."
And 2 Corinthians 5:21 tells us that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
This is the Gospel.
Not that your sin is insignificant.
But that Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Not that holiness doesn't matter.
But that holiness grows from belonging to Christ, not from purchasing His acceptance through your performance.
Not that repentance is optional.
But that the mercy of God calls us to repentance and gives us hope when we turn to Him.
And perhaps one of the most beautiful pictures of that mercy is found in Luke 15.
Jesus tells the story of a son who demands his inheritance, leaves home, and wastes his possessions in reckless living.
Eventually, he is hungry.
Desperate.
Humiliated.
And alone.
The boy who once believed freedom meant escaping his father's house now finds himself longing for food given to pigs.
Then Scripture says something extraordinary.
"He came to himself." (Luke 15:17, KJV)
There is a moment when sin's promises begin to collapse.
When the excitement wears off.
When the pleasure stops distracting you.
When you finally see what your choices have been costing.
And you realize you have been starving while running away from the very place where you could have been fed.
So the son decides to return.
He prepares a confession.
He knows he has sinned.
He does not demand restoration as something he deserves.
But while he is still a great way off, his father sees him.
And runs.
And embraces him.
And welcomes him home.
The father does not celebrate the son's rebellion.
He celebrates his return.
"This my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." (Luke 15:24, KJV)
That is not a picture of cheap grace.
That is a picture of undeserved mercy.
And while this parable must be understood in its own context, its message speaks powerfully to every sinner who has begun believing that coming home is no longer possible.
Maybe you've wasted years.
Maybe you've betrayed trust.
Maybe you've become someone you never imagined you could become.
Maybe you have been hiding behind church attendance, ministry involvement, and carefully chosen Bible verses while privately feeding a habit that is slowly hardening your heart.
Then stop pretending.
Not because you are beyond hope.
But because you don't have to keep hiding from the One who calls sinners to repentance.
Come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Turn around.
Receive the mercy of Christ.
And begin walking in the freedom He commands and supplies.
But there is one more thing we need to understand about lust.
Even when a person has addressed loneliness, stress, rejection, or insecurity, the struggle may not simply disappear.
Why?
Because lust is not always a symptom of emotional pain.
It can also be an expression of the sinful desires Scripture calls us to put to death.
Colossians 3:5 commands believers to put to death what belongs to their earthly nature, including sexual immorality, impurity, passion, and evil desire.
The Christian life is not simply a journey of self-discovery.
It is a life of self-denial, Spirit-enabled obedience, and transformation into the likeness of Christ.
Jesus says in Luke 9:23:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." (KJV)
Daily.
Not just on the day you got baptized.
Not just when you first believed.
Not just after a powerful worship service.
Daily.
Some days, following Jesus means refusing something your body strongly wants.
Some days, it means surrendering a fantasy you have secretly treasured.
Some days, it means accepting that a relationship must end because it is drawing you away from obedience.
Some days, it means sitting with loneliness instead of numbing it.
Some days, it means praying through tears because your emotions haven't caught up with your convictions.
And some days, faithfulness looks very ordinary.
Going to bed.
Putting the phone away.
Opening your Bible.
Calling someone you trust.
Leaving the room.
Refusing to answer the message.
Choosing not to look again.
No dramatic music.
No visible miracle.
No applause.
Just a believer, strengthened by grace, choosing obedience when disobedience is available.
And heaven's approval is not measured by how spectacular that moment appears to other people.
Your secret obedience matters.
Not because God loves you more when you succeed.
But because the God who loves you is worthy of your obedience.
Galatians 5:16 says:
"Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh." (KJV)
The instruction is not merely to stare at sin until you become strong enough to defeat it.
It is to walk in the Spirit.
To cultivate a life increasingly shaped by God's Word, prayer, fellowship, worship, confession, and obedience.
To stop feeding the flesh while starving the soul.
To recognize that lasting Christian transformation is not accomplished through shame alone.
It is the work of God's grace as we actively respond in faith.
And here is the question I want you to carry beyond this article:
When lust comes knocking, what is it asking you to give up in exchange for what it promises?
Your integrity?
Your peace?
Your marriage?
Your honesty?
Your ability to see another person with dignity?
Your willingness to trust God?
Your spiritual sensitivity?
Your freedom?
Because lust often advertises what it can give you while concealing what surrendering to it may cost.
It offers a moment.
Then asks for another.
And another.
And another.
Until the thing you once called a choice begins to feel like a chain.
But Jesus offers something radically different.
He does not promise that every desire will vanish the moment you pray.
He does not promise that the Christian life will be free from temptation.
He promises Himself.
His grace.
His truth.
His Spirit.
His presence.
And eternal life through faith in Him.
The One who said "I thirst" while hanging on the cross (John 19:28) is the same Savior who invites the thirsty to come to Him (John 7:37).
Those passages have distinct contexts, but together they draw our attention to the suffering Savior and His gracious invitation.
Jesus knows what it is to suffer.
He knows what it is to be tempted.
He knows what it is to be rejected.
And unlike every false savior you have ever chased, He does not exploit your need.
He gives Himself for sinners.
So perhaps tonight your most important prayer is not simply, "God, take away this feeling."
Perhaps it is:

"Lord, show me what I've been seeking apart from You. Expose what is sinful. Heal what is wounded. Correct what is false. Teach me to desire what is good. And give me the courage to obey You even when my feelings resist."
That is a prayer worth praying.
Not because it guarantees an instant transformation.
But because it expresses a heart turning toward the only Savior who can truly redeem it.
And if you are struggling right now, please don't turn this article into another weapon against yourself.
Let it become an invitation to honesty.
You do not need to announce the details of your private struggle to strangers online.
You do not need to expose another person's sins.
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
But you can acknowledge that you need Christ.
You can ask for prayer.
You can reach out to someone trustworthy.
You can take the next faithful step.
Or, if you're still in the middle of the battle, simply write:
Not as a performance.
Not as proof of salvation.
But as a small, honest acknowledgment that you don't want to keep fighting alone.
Someone reading silently may need to know that repentance is possible, that growth can happen, and that the grace of Jesus Christ is not an empty religious slogan.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who looks completely fine.
They post family photos.
They laugh at jokes.
They share inspirational quotes.
They attend church.
And yet, when everyone goes to sleep, they're fighting a battle nobody sees.
And if someone specific comes to mind, consider tagging them with care, or sending the article privately if that would better honor their dignity.
Don't use the message to embarrass someone.
Not because these words have power in themselves, but because the Scriptures we've considered deserve to be revisited when temptation feels louder than truth.
Return to Matthew 5.
Read John 4.
Meditate on Luke 15.
Pray through Romans 8.
Remember 1 John 1:9.
And keep coming back to Christ.
It's about following the real Jesus.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who feel spiritually exhausted, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who are still searching for truth.
Because the Gospel is not merely for people who already know how to sound religious.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.
It does not purchase forgiveness, spiritual favor, salvation, or a blessing.
But Scripture does encourage believers to support faithful Gospel ministry voluntarily, generously, and with discernment.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
It can help us reach people who may be silently wrestling with the very struggles discussed here.
There is no pressure to give what you cannot afford.
Those free resources reflect an important conviction behind this ministry:
The Word of God should never be treated as merchandise that only paying supporters deserve to encounter.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Our mission is to keep pointing people to it.
Send it to a struggling believer.
Pray for the people who will read it.
Because sometimes a message about a hidden struggle reaches someone at the very moment they're considering surrendering to it again.
And sometimes the reminder that Jesus still receives repentant sinners becomes the beginning of a very different decision.
Does lust always want something?
Yes.
Lust reaches for something it believes will satisfy.
Sometimes that desire is intensified by loneliness, fear, insecurity, pain, or exhaustion.
Sometimes it is driven by an appetite that has been repeatedly indulged.
Sometimes several of those things are happening at once.
But whatever the circumstances, sinful lust must be confronted with truth, repentance, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest answer to our sin is not simply finding a more effective distraction.
It is being reconciled to God through His Son and learning to live as someone who belongs to Him.
Maybe you've spent years trying to prove that you're strong enough.
Strong enough not to look.
Strong enough not to fantasize.
Strong enough not to fall.
Strong enough to keep your secrets hidden.
But salvation has never depended on proving that you are strong enough to save yourself.
It depends on Jesus Christ, who is mighty to save.
You may still have difficult days ahead.
You may need to rebuild trust.
You may need to make painful changes.
You may need help.
You will need to keep choosing repentance and faith.
But your story does not have to remain trapped in the chapter where your sin became visible.
Peter denied Jesus.
And the risen Christ restored him.
The Samaritan woman had a complicated relational history.
And Jesus revealed Himself to her.
The prodigal son wasted what he had been given.
And his father welcomed him home when he returned.
These are not identical stories.
But each reminds us that failure does not place repentant sinners beyond the reach of God's mercy.
And at the center of our hope stands something greater than every testimony.
The cross.
The empty tomb.
The living Christ.
So tonight, if the old hunger returns, remember that you are not required to obey every desire that demands your attention.
You can stop.
You can pray.
You can seek help.
You can flee temptation.
You can choose the light.
And if you have fallen, you can repent and come to Christ without pretending your sin was harmless or believing His mercy is exhausted.
Because the most beautiful transformation isn't merely when someone stops pursuing what was destroying them.
It's when they begin loving the Savior who gave Himself to redeem them.
The desire that once led you into hiding does not have to write the final sentence of your story. Jesus Christ is still calling sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
